definition: To collect and store away a large supply of something, often secretly or more than is needed.
example: Before the long winter, the villagers began to hoard firewood and sacks of dried beans.
nuance: Unlike stockpile, hoard suggests excess or selfish secrecy; don't confuse it with horde, which means a large crowd.
prompt: A grocery store announces that paper towels will be scarce next month.
options: Worried shoppers began to hoard paper towels, filling their carts with a dozen packs each.
A crowd of shoppers began to hoard through the doors the moment the manager unlocked them.
Generous customers chose to hoard their extra rolls by handing them out to elderly neighbors.
One cautious shopper decided to hoard a single roll, just enough to get through the week.
reasons: Grabbing far more than they need and storing it against a shortage is exactly this behavior.
Pouring in as a mass of people describes a horde, a look-alike word for a crowd.
Giving supplies away is the reverse of keeping a stash for yourself.
Buying only what you need lacks the excess the word implies.

practice.prompt: In an art class, one student keeps the best supplies to herself.
options: Lena would hoard one marker for a minute and then return it to the shared bin.
Instead of sharing, Lena tended to hoard the brightest markers in her desk drawer.
To be fair to classmates, Lena would hoard the markers by passing them around the table.
When the bell rang, the students would hoard toward the supply closet in a noisy rush.
reasons: Briefly borrowing one item is not building up a hidden supply.
Hiding away more than her share of supplies shows selfish stockpiling.
Passing supplies around spreads them out instead of keeping them back.
A rushing group of people is a horde; the sound-alike verb means storing things.
